Direct Acceleration of Stochastic Root-Finding
Without Variance Reduction and Regularization

TaeHo Yoon*    Nicolas Loizou*
Abstract

Acceleration for deterministic root-finding problems has been extensively studied in recent years; specifically, the anchor-based, or Halpern-type methods achieve optimal convergence rates with respect to the operator norm. However, acceleration via these methods does not directly carry over to stochastic setting due to accumulation of errors, unless one enforces diminishing variance via increasing batch sizes or variance reduction techniques. In this work, we show that another class of acceleration, namely the dual-anchor mechanism, extends to the stochastic setting without such error accumulation, in contrast to anchor-based algorithms. Consequently, we cleanly achieve 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) complexity with iteration-independent batch size, without any variance reduction or double-loop recursive regularization, for stochastic root-finding (resp. fixed-point) problems with cocoercivity (resp. square-nonexpansivity) in expectation. For strongly monotone operators, the same algorithm attains a sharper 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) complexity, nearly matching the lower bound in terms of ϵ\epsilon-dependence.

1 Introduction

Root-finding problems for an operator F:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{F}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, stated as

findx∈RdF⁡(x)=0,\displaystyle\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\text{find}}\quad{\mathbb{F}}(x)=0, (1)

generalize minimization problems and have been studied under distinct formulations including monotone inclusion [36, 42, 3, 43], minimax optimization [38, 19, 33, 13, 35, 31], equilibrium search [47, 17, 46], or fixed-point problems [24, 34, 21, 51, 45]. In the past few years, there have been significant developments in accelerated algorithms for reducing the squared operator/residual norm with the optimal ‖F⁡(xk)‖2=𝒪⁡(1/k2)\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{k})\right\|^{2}={\mathcal{O}}(1/k^{2}) rate [29, 16, 22, 40, 56, 27]. A recurring message from the optimization literature, however, is that deterministic acceleration is often brittle under oracle errors; in the stochastic setting where F​(x)=E​[F^​(x,ξ)]{\mathbb{F}}(x)=\mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi)\right] and the algorithm uses F^​(x,ξ)\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi), error may accumulate quickly with these accelerated methods and break their fast convergence from the noiseless setting. Consequently, for stochastic optimization problems, taking advantage of the study of acceleration was not straightforward—it required decaying oracle inexactness, variance reduction, restart mechanisms, or stronger assumptions on the problem [15, 18, 28, 10]. Specifically for stochastic monotone inclusion problems, stochastic Halpern iteration and accelerated (anchored) extragradient type analyses suffered precisely from these issues [27, 10, 9].

We take a different viewpoint toward handling stochastic instability. Recent work [54] showed that the acceleration mechanism in fixed-point and minimax problems is not unique: besides anchor-based algorithms [29, 22, 56, 27, 49], there exist their H-dual algorithms, which display materially different update rules but share exactly the same deterministic last-iterate rate with the optimal anchor-based acceleration. Hence, the deterministic worst-case complexity alone does not identify a single preferred accelerated method. In this paper, we demonstrate that the stochastic extension can break this tie: the Stochastic Dual Optimal Halpern Method (S-Dual-OHM) attains E⁡[‖F⁡(xN−1)‖]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1})\right\|\right]\leq\epsilon with 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) oracle complexity, with iteration complexity N=𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)N={\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1}) and with constant mini-batch size 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}). This is done cleanly and more directly without assuming diminishing variance or using variance reduction techniques, which is not what stochastic anchoring methods were capable of [27, 10, 9].

In our view, this result has a conceptual implication beyond simply providing another efficient stochastic algorithm. It challenges the folklore view that acceleration, as studied in deterministic optimization, is brittle and incompatible with stochastic noise. Equivalently, optimal deterministic methods can behave very differently under stochastic perturbations, and selecting the right representation of acceleration may enable the design of efficient stochastic algorithms.

Contributions.

We summarize our main contributions as follows.

  • ⋄\diamond

    We show that under cocoercivity of F{\mathbb{F}} in expectation, our proposed S-Dual-OHM with mini-batching over F^​(⋅,ξ)\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(\cdot;\xi) with constant step-size α∈(0,2L]\alpha\in\left(0,\frac{2}{L}\right] and constant batch size B=𝒪⁡(ϵ−2)B={\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) achieves the bound E⁡[‖F⁡(xN−1)‖]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1})\right\|\right]\leq\epsilon within N=𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)N={\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1}) iterations. The resulting total oracle complexity 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}), to the best of our knowledge, has not been achieved in prior work without variance reduction or double-loop regularization techniques (Table 1).

  • ⋄\diamond

    We show that when F{\mathbb{F}} is additionally strongly monotone, the same S-Dual-OHM algorithm can be early-stopped in k=𝒪~​(L/μ​log⁡ϵ−1)k=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\nicefrac{{L}}{{\mu}}\log\epsilon^{-1}) iterations to attain E⁡[‖F⁡(xk)‖]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{k})\right\|\right]\leq\epsilon. This yields the oracle complexity 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}), which has near-optimal dependence on ϵ\epsilon.

  • ⋄\diamond

    We provide numerical experiments demonstrating that Dual-OHM is indeed more robust to stochastic noise than Halpern iteration, and that S-Dual-OHM can effectively solve stochastic root-finding problems.

2 Related Work

Fixed-point problems, Halpern iteration and acceleration.

For fixed-point problems

findx∈Rdx=T⁡(x),\displaystyle\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\text{find}}\quad x={\mathbb{T}}(x), (2)

with a nonexpansive operator T:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{T}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, the Halpern iteration xk+1=βk​x0+(1−βk)​T​xkx_{k+1}=\beta_{k}x_{0}+(1-\beta_{k}){\mathbb{T}}x_{k} has been studied over a long history in the literature [21, 51], and has been found to provide accelerated worst-case convergence rate ‖xk−T⁡(xk)‖=𝒪⁡(1/k)\left\|x_{k}-{\mathbb{T}}(x_{k})\right\|={\mathcal{O}}(1/k) with βk=𝒪⁡(1/k)\beta_{k}={\mathcal{O}}(1/k) [45, 16, 29, 22, 26]. The best choice βk=1k+2\beta_{k}=\frac{1}{k+2}, due to [29, 22], was later shown to yield an optimal rate ‖xk−T⁡(xk)‖2≤4​‖x0−x⋆‖2(k+1)2\left\|x_{k}-{\mathbb{T}}(x_{k})\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{4\left\|x_{0}-x_{\star}\right\|^{2}}{(k+1)^{2}}, exactly matching the lower bound [40]. More recently, it was discovered that the same exact optimal rate for a fixed finite horizon NN can be achieved by distinct types of acceleration forming an infinite family of algorithms [55] including Dual-OHM [54], the basis of this work.

Acceleration of minimax optimization and monotone inclusion.

Minimax optimization with convex-concave objective can be recast into monotone inclusion, i.e., root-finding problem (1) with saddle gradient operator F{\mathbb{F}}, which is a monotone operator [42, 17]. Some early works including [44, 16] first connected Halpern acceleration to these problems, and [16] achieved near-optimal complexity for Lipschitz continuous monotone inclusions. The remaining logarithmic gap was removed by the Extra Anchored Gradient algorithm [56], and the so-called anchor acceleration for minimax optimization and monotone inclusion has been studied extensively since then [27, 49, 57, 48, 11, 5, 1, 25]. Several works proposed its extension via distinct interpretation in connection with Nesterov momentum [6, 50]. On the other hand, the dual-anchor acceleration analogous to Dual-OHM from fixed-point problems is achievable in this setting as well [54].

Residual-reducing algorithms for stochastic fixed-point and monotone inclusion problems.

The Fast Extragradient algorithm [27], an anchor-based accelerated minimax algorithm, was proposed with its stochastic extension under the assumption that the operator’s variance at kk-th iteration diminishes at the order of 𝒪⁡(1/k){\mathcal{O}}(1/k). Then [10] showed that stochastic Halpern iteration and its minimax variants, combined with PAGE variance reduction [28] can reduce the complexity of achieving E⁡[‖F⁡(xk)‖]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{k})\right\|\right]\leq\epsilon to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}), which could be further improved to 𝒪~​(n+n​ϵ−1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n+\sqrt{n}\epsilon^{-1}) [9] in the finite-sum setting where F{\mathbb{F}} is the average of n=o⁡(ϵ−3)n=o(\epsilon^{-3}) sample operators. Near-optimal complexity of 𝒪~​(ϵ−2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}) for stochastic monotone inclusion has been achieved in [12] with the matching Ω⁡(ϵ−2)\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}) lower bound via more sophisticated recursive anchoring (regularization) algorithm. On another line of work, [7, 41, 8] studied stochastic Krasnosel’skiĭ–Mann or Halpern iterations in general normed spaces, where the lower bound of Ω⁡(ϵ−3)\Omega(\epsilon^{-3}) was established [8].

Broader view of extending acceleration to stochastic settings.

In smooth convex minimization, it is now standard that accelerated methods are fragile to persistent oracle error: preserving acceleration under stochasticity typically requires either variance reduction or catalyst-type outer–inner regularization [15, 30, 2]. A similar viewpoint has been adopted for monotone root-finding problems in prior works [10, 9, 12]. Our approach departs from this line of work. Rather than stabilizing Halpern-type acceleration by additional variance-reduction or regularization, we leverage the fact that deterministic acceleration is not unique, and there exist distinct optimal accelerated algorithms with the same worst-case deterministic rate. We deliver the new observation that among them, Dual-OHM is intrinsically less sensitive to stochastic perturbations than Halpern-type algorithms, enabling direct stochastic extension.

3 Preliminaries and Assumptions

In this section, we establish some necessary preliminary concepts for subsequent analysis.

3.1 Monotonicity, cocoercivity, and nonexpansiveness of operators

We say that an operator F:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{F}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is

  • -

    Monotone if ⟨F⁡(x)−F⁡(y),x−y⟩≥0\left\langle{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y),x-y\right\rangle\geq 0 for all x,y∈Rdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}

  • -

    μ\mu-strongly monotone if ⟨F⁡(x)−F⁡(y),x−y⟩≥μ​‖x−y‖2\left\langle{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y),x-y\right\rangle\geq\mu\left\|x-y\right\|^{2} for all x,y∈Rdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}

  • -

    MM-Lipschitz if ‖F⁡(x)−F⁡(y)‖≤M⁡‖x−y‖\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y)\right\|\leq M\left\|x-y\right\| for all x,y∈Rdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}

  • -

    1/L\nicefrac{{1}}{{L}}-Cocoercive if ⟨F⁡(x)−F⁡(y),x−y⟩≥1L​‖F⁡(x)−F⁡(y)‖2\left\langle{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y),x-y\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{L}\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y)\right\|^{2} for all x,y∈Rdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}

where μ,M,L>0\mu,M,L>0. In particular, 1/L\nicefrac{{1}}{{L}}-cocoercivity implies monotonicity and LL-Lipschitzness, but not vice versa. If F{\mathbb{F}} is MM-Lipschitz and μ\mu-strongly monotone, then it is 1/L\nicefrac{{1}}{{L}}-cocoercive with L=M2/μL=\nicefrac{{M^{2}}}{{\mu}} [17]. When F{\mathbb{F}} is 1/L\nicefrac{{1}}{{L}}-cocoercive, the problem (1) can be recast into a fixed-point problem (2) where T=I−α​F:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is nonexpansive, i.e., 11-Lipschitz for 0<α≤2L0<\alpha\leq\frac{2}{L} [3, Proposition 4.39], where I:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{I}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is the identity operator. This is because

Zer⁡(F):={x∈Rd|F⁡(x)=0}={x∈Rd|T⁡(x)=x}:=Fix⁡(T).\mathrm{Zer}\,({\mathbb{F}}):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\,|\,{\mathbb{F}}(x)=0\}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\,|\,{\mathbb{T}}(x)=x\}:=\mathrm{Fix}\,({\mathbb{T}}).

Given an unconstrained minimax problem

minimizeu∈Rm​maximizev∈Rn​Φ​(u,v)\displaystyle\underset{u\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}{\text{minimize}}\,\,\underset{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}{\text{maximize}}\,\,\Phi(u,v) (3)

with a convex-concave (resp. μ\mu-strongly-convex-strongly-concave) and MM-smooth Φ:Rm×Rn→R\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, its saddle operator

F⁡(u,v)=(∇uΦ​(u,v),−∇vΦ​(u,v)){\mathbb{F}}(u,v)=(\nabla_{u}\Phi(u,v),-\nabla_{v}\Phi(u,v))

is monotone (resp. μ\mu-strongly monotone) and MM-Lipschitz [17].

3.2 Stochastic oracle models

We consider an unbiased stochastic operator oracle with bounded variance.

3.1Stochastic operator oracle.

Given x∈Rdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, one can query F^​(x,ξ)\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi) such that

E⁡[F^​(x,ξ)]=F⁡(x),E⁡[‖F^​(x,ξ)−F⁡(x)‖2]≤σ2.\mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi)\right]={\mathbb{F}}(x),\qquad\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi)-{\mathbb{F}}(x)\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}.

For our main result (Theorem 4.1), we additionally assume the following condition.

3.2Cocoercivity in expectation.

For any x,y∈Rdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have

⟨F⁡(x)−F⁡(y),x−y⟩≥E⁡[1L​‖F^​(x,ξ)−F^​(y,ξ)‖2].\left\langle{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y),x-y\right\rangle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{L}\left\|\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi)-\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(y;\xi)\right\|^{2}\right].

This condition holds for some natural cases, including: (i) stochastic oracle with additive noise F^​(x,ξ)=F⁡(x)+ζ⁡(ξ)\widehat{{\mathbb{F}}}(x;\xi)={\mathbb{F}}(x)+\zeta(\xi), where the noise ζ⁡(ξ)\zeta(\xi) is independent of xx, (ii) finite sum or expectation models where each sample operator is 1/L\nicefrac{{1}}{{L}}-cocoercive, and as its special case, (iii) sample operators that are each μ\mu-strongly monotone (μ>0\mu>0) and MM-Lipschitz, which implies sample-wise cocoercivity [17]. Note that 3.2 does not capture general monotone and Lipschitz sample operators or the cases where the noise ζ⁡(ξ)\zeta(\xi) depends on xx. Similar assumptions or even stronger samplewise cocoercivity have been commonly used in stochastic optimization [39, 2, 32, 37, 4, 58, 52, 14, 9].

Given batch size B≥1B\geq 1, we denote Fℬ​(x)=1B​∑b=1BF^​(x,ξb){\mathbb{F}}_{\mathcal{B}}(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi_{b}), where ξb\xi_{b} are conditionally independent samples given xx and ℬ={ξ1,…,ξB}{\mathcal{B}}=\{\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{B}\}. Then Fℬ​(x){\mathbb{F}}_{\mathcal{B}}(x) is an unbiased estimator of F⁡(x){\mathbb{F}}(x) with E⁡[‖Fℬ​(x)−F⁡(x)‖2]≤σ2B\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}_{\mathcal{B}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(x)\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B} and ⟨F⁡(x)−F⁡(y),x−y⟩≥E⁡[1L​‖Fℬ​(x)−Fℬ​(y)‖2]\left\langle{\mathbb{F}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}(y),x-y\right\rangle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{L}\left\|{\mathbb{F}}_{\mathcal{B}}(x)-{\mathbb{F}}_{\mathcal{B}}(y)\right\|^{2}\right] by Jensen’s inequality. For 0<α≤2L0<\alpha\leq\frac{2}{L}, if we let T^​(⋅,ξ)=I−α​F^​(⋅,ξ)\widehat{\mathbb{T}}(\cdot;\xi)={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(\cdot;\xi) and Tℬ​(⋅)=1B​∑b=1BT^​(⋅,ξb){\mathbb{T}}_{\mathcal{B}}(\cdot)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\widehat{\mathbb{T}}(\cdot;\xi_{b}), then these are unbiased estimators of the nonexpansive T=I−α​F{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}} with variance bounds α2​σ2\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2} and α2​σ2B\frac{\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B}, respectively. Furthermore, we have: E⁡[‖Tℬ​(x)−Tℬ​(y)‖2]≤‖x−y‖2\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{T}}_{\mathcal{B}}(x)-{\mathbb{T}}_{\mathcal{B}}(y)\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\left\|x-y\right\|^{2} (square-nonexpansivity in expectation).

3.3 Known acceleration in fixed-point problems and its extension

Our general strategy is to reformulate (1) with cocoercive F{\mathbb{F}} into (2) with T=I−α​F{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}} and build upon deterministic acceleration results. Consider the following algorithms: given y0∈Rdy_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

yk+1=1k+2​y0+k+1k+2​T​yk\displaystyle y_{k+1}=\frac{1}{k+2}y_{0}+\frac{k+1}{k+2}{\mathbb{T}}y_{k} (OHM)

and, with the convention T​y−1=y0{\mathbb{T}}y_{-1}=y_{0},

yk+1=yk+N−k−1N−k​(T​yk−T​yk−1)\displaystyle y_{k+1}=y_{k}+\frac{N-k-1}{N-k}\left({\mathbb{T}}y_{k}-{\mathbb{T}}y_{k-1}\right) (Dual-OHM)

Here, OHM is an anytime algorithm whose update is defined for all k=0,1,…k=0,1,\dots, while for Dual-OHM, the terminal iteration number NN is fixed, and the update is defined only for k=0,…,N−2k=0,\dots,N-2. This is a substantive distinction that makes the two algorithms behave differently under stochastic extension (see the discussion in Section 4.1.1 for further details).

3.3Deterministic acceleration [29, 22, 54].

For a nonexpansive operator T:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{T}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} with a fixed point y⋆∈Fix​Ty_{\star}\in\mathrm{Fix}\,{\mathbb{T}} and N≥2N\geq 2, both OHM and Dual-OHM exhibit the rate

‖yN−1−T⁡(yN−1)‖2≤4​‖y0−y⋆‖2N2.\left\|y_{N-1}-{\mathbb{T}}(y_{N-1})\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{4\left\|y_{0}-y_{\star}\right\|^{2}}{N^{2}}.

With T=I−α​F{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}} and α=1L\alpha=\frac{1}{L}, Proposition 3.3 shows that ‖F⁡(yN−1)‖=‖yN−1−T⁡(yN−1)‖α≤ϵ\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(y_{N-1})\right\|=\frac{\left\|y_{N-1}-{\mathbb{T}}(y_{N-1})\right\|}{\alpha}\leq\epsilon is achieved in 𝒪⁡(L​Dϵ){\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{LD}{\epsilon}\right) iterations, where D=‖y0−y⋆‖D=\left\|y_{0}-y_{\star}\right\|.

3.4Cai et al. [10], Informal.

Stochastic OHM (S-OHM), which has the update rule xk+1=1k+2​x0+k+1k+2​Tℬk​(xk)x_{k+1}=\frac{1}{k+2}x_{0}+\frac{k+1}{k+2}{\mathbb{T}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k}), maintains the deterministic iteration bound N=𝒪⁡(L⁡‖x0−x⋆‖/ϵ)N={\mathcal{O}}(L\left\|x_{0}-x_{\star}\right\|/\epsilon) if E​‖Fℬk​(xk)−F⁡(xk)‖2≲ϵ2k\mathbb{E}\left\|{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k})-{\mathbb{F}}(x_{k})\right\|^{2}\lesssim\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{k}. Simple mini-batching with |ℬk|=Θ⁡(k​ϵ−2)|{\mathcal{B}}_{k}|=\Theta(k\epsilon^{-2}) yields 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-4}) stochastic oracle complexity, and using PAGE variance reduction, this can be reduced to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}).

4 Stochastic Dual-Anchor Acceleration

In this section, we analyze Stochastic Dual-OHM (S-Dual-OHM): with Tℬ−1​(x−1)=x0{\mathbb{T}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{-1}}(x_{-1})=x_{0},

xk+1=xk+N−k−1N−k​(Tℬk​(xk)−Tℬk−1​(xk−1))\displaystyle x_{k+1}=x_{k}+\frac{N-k-1}{N-k}\left({\mathbb{T}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k})-{\mathbb{T}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k-1}}(x_{k-1})\right) (S-Dual-OHM)

for k=0,…,N−2k=0,\dots,N-2, and present the following main result of this paper.

4.1.

Consider the root-finding problem (1) with a solution x⋆x_{\star}, satisfying Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2. Then for 0<α≤2L0<\alpha\leq\frac{2}{L}, S-Dual-OHM with Tℬk=I−α​Fℬk{\mathbb{T}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}} with |ℬk|≡B|{\mathcal{B}}_{k}|\equiv B satisfies

E​[‖F⁡(xN−1)‖]2≤E⁡[‖F⁡(xN−1)‖2]≤4​‖x0−x⋆‖2α2​N2+6​σ2B.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1})\right\|\right]^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1})\right\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{4\left\|x_{0}-x_{\star}\right\|^{2}}{\alpha^{2}N^{2}}+\frac{6\sigma^{2}}{B}.

This shows that we will have E⁡[‖F⁡(xN−1)‖]≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1})\right\|\right]\leq\epsilon with N=Θ⁡(1/ϵ)N=\Theta(1/\epsilon) and B=Θ⁡(1/ϵ2)B=\Theta(1/\epsilon^{2}), so in total, 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ3){\mathcal{O}}(1/\epsilon^{3}) oracle complexity. This also proves an equivalent bound on the expected fixed-point residual E​[‖xN−1−T⁡(xN−1)‖]2≤4​‖x0−x⋆‖2N2+6​α2​σ2B\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|x_{N-1}-{\mathbb{T}}(x_{N-1})\right\|\right]^{2}\leq\frac{4\left\|x_{0}-x_{\star}\right\|^{2}}{N^{2}}+\frac{6\alpha^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B}. While we defer technical details to Appendix A, we provide the outline of key arguments below. Then, we show that with the additional assumption of strong monotonicity of F{\mathbb{F}}, the total complexity can be reduced to 𝒪~​(1/ϵ2)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\epsilon^{2}) with early stopping.

4.1 Proof outline for Theorem 4.1

We start with showing the identity characterizing the S-Dual-OHM algorithm.

4.2.

For S-Dual-OHM with Tℬk=I−α​Fℬk{\mathbb{T}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}, the following identity holds:

4.1.1 Intuition for why S-Dual-OHM is stable under noise

The previous analysis shows that the net accumulation of error in S-Dual-OHM is proportional to ∑j=1N−1λN,j=α⁡(N−1)2=𝒪⁡(N)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\lambda_{N,j}=\frac{\alpha(N-1)}{2}={\mathcal{O}}(N). On the other hand, stochastic OHM satisfies the similar identity

0\displaystyle 0 =(N−1)​α24​‖F⁡(xN−1)‖2+α2​⟨F⁡(xN−1),xN−1−x0⟩+∑j=1N−1νj+1,j​𝒬j+1,j\displaystyle=\frac{(N-1)\alpha^{2}}{4}\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1})\right\|^{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}\left\langle{\mathbb{F}}(x_{N-1}),x_{N-1}-x_{0}\right\rangle+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\nu_{j+1,j}{\mathcal{Q}}_{j+1,j}

where 𝒬j+1,j=⟨xj−1−xj,Fℬj−1​(xj−1)−Fℬj​(xj)⟩−α2​‖Fℬj−1​(xj−1)−Fℬj​(xj)‖2{\mathcal{Q}}_{j+1,j}=\left\langle x_{j-1}-x_{j},{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{j-1}}(x_{j-1})-{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{j}}(x_{j})\right\rangle-\frac{\alpha}{2}\left\|{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{j-1}}(x_{j-1})-{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{j}}(x_{j})\right\|^{2} but with νj+1,j=α​j​(j+1)2​N\nu_{j+1,j}=\frac{\alpha j(j+1)}{2N}. Here each 𝒬j+1,j{\mathcal{Q}}_{j+1,j} is not nonnegative, but contributes a negative lower bound proportional to σ2\sigma^{2} in expectation, which then gets multiplied with ∑j=1N−1νj+1,j=Θ⁡(N2)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\nu_{j+1,j}=\Theta(N^{2}) and the resulting error term is no longer controllable as in Theorem 4.1. This is a central difference that makes the dual-anchor mechanism more amenable to stochastic extension than anchoring. A concurrent work [53] has also provided a related theory that the sum of weights associated with inequalities used in the convergence proof measures a fixed-point algorithm’s robustness to oracle noise, albeit in deterministic setting.

A complementary interpretation is that OHM is an anytime optimal algorithm, achieving the rate ‖F⁡(xk−1)‖2≤4​‖x0−x⋆‖2α2​k2\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{k-1})\right\|^{2}\leq\frac{4\left\|x_{0}-x_{\star}\right\|^{2}}{\alpha^{2}k^{2}} for all k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dots. This means that OHM must maintain the optimal guarantee at every iteration, forcing it to exploit the geometric property of F{\mathbb{F}}, i.e. cocoercivity, throughout the trajectory. Its analysis is therefore more tightly tuned to the exact problem class and is more easily disrupted by oracle noise. Dual-OHM, by contrast, is optimized only for the prescribed last iterate and does not suffer from the same accumulation of errors.

5 Numerical Experiments

We provide numerical evaluations to demonstrate that the dual-anchor mechanism is indeed preferable to anchoring (Halpern algorithms) under stochasticity, and compare the empirical performance of S-Dual-OHM with prior algorithms for stochastic monotone inclusions/fixed-point problems. We consider three distinct problems: the worst-case nonexpansive fixed-point operator designed by [40], a finite-sum cocoercive operator using uniform random vectors from the unit sphere, and a strongly-convex–strongly-concave minimax problem with Huber-type regularizers following [56, 12]. All experiments were run on a MacBook Air with Apple M3 Chip and 24GB Memory.

Baseline algorithms.

We consider the simple algorithm xk+1=xk−α​Fℬk​(xk)x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k}), which we call Stochastic Gradient Descent-Ascent (SGDA) following the nomenclature of the minimax optimization literature. We consider the Stochastic Extragradient (SEG) with the update rule

xk+1/2=xk−α​Fℬk​(xk),xk+1=xk−α​Fℬk+1/2​(xk+1/2).x_{k+1/2}=x_{k}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k}),\quad x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k+1/2}}(x_{k+1/2}).

Next, we consider the naive stochastic extension of OHM: xk+1=1k+2​x0+k+1k+2​(xk−α​Fℬk​(xk))x_{k+1}=\frac{1}{k+2}x_{0}+\frac{k+1}{k+2}\left(x_{k}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k})\right), using the same constant mini-batch size as S-Dual-OHM. We refer to this algorithm as S-OHM (with constant BB). This is included to isolate the effect of using the dual-anchor update rather than the usual anchor acceleration and directly contrast the two mechanisms.

We also include the algorithms carefully designed for reducing the expected last-iterate residual. First, the Halpern-PAGE algorithm from [10] uses the S-OHM update but replaces Fℬk​(xk){\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}}(x_{k}) by a PAGE-type estimator which uses a larger batch size s1s_{1} with probability pk=min⁡{1,2k+2}p_{k}=\min\left\{1,\frac{2}{k+2}\right\} and otherwise uses a sample operator difference with batch size s2s_{2}. Second, we use the single-loop simplification of RAIN algorithm from [12] used in their experiments, which can be written as

zk+1/2=zk−η⁡(F^​(zk,ξk)+rk​(zk)),zk+1=zk−η⁡(F^​(zk+1/2,ξk+1/2)+rk​(zk+1/2))z_{k+1/2}=z_{k}-\eta\bigl(\widehat{{\mathbb{F}}}(z_{k};\xi_{k})+r_{k}(z_{k})\bigr),\qquad z_{k+1}=z_{k}-\eta\bigl(\widehat{{\mathbb{F}}}(z_{k+1/2};\xi_{k+1/2})+r_{k}(z_{k+1/2})\bigr)

where rk​(x)=λ​γ​(Sk​x−mk),Sk=∑t<k(1+γ)t,mk=∑t<k(1+γ)t​ztr_{k}(x)=\lambda\gamma(S_{k}x-m_{k}),S_{k}=\sum_{t<k}(1+\gamma)^{t},m_{k}=\sum_{t<k}(1+\gamma)^{t}z_{t}, and η,λ,γ>0\eta,\lambda,\gamma>0 are hyperparameters. Finally, Halpern-VR-Finite from [9] is similar to Halpern-PAGE but applicable only to finite sum problems of the form F=1n​∑i=1nF⁡(⋅,ξi){\mathbb{F}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{F}}(\cdot;\xi_{i}) and uses either full-batch (true) operator F{\mathbb{F}} or batches of size ⌈n⌉\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil.

We tune all baseline algorithms and S-Dual-OHM under the same total sample budget Q=N​BQ=NB via grid search, where computing Fℬk{\mathbb{F}}_{{\mathcal{B}}_{k}} with |ℬk|=B|{\mathcal{B}}_{k}|=B counts as BB operator evaluations. The only hyperparameter BB for S-Dual-OHM is tuned over B∈{1,10,20,50,100}B\in\{1,10,20,50,100\}, and S-OHM (Constant BB) is then run with the same selected BB.11 1 While this emphasizes the distinction between the anchor and the dual-anchor updates, for fully controlled comparison, we additionally provide experiments where BB for S-OHM is tuned separately in Appendix B. The Halpern-PAGE parameters are tuned over s1∈{1,10,20,50,100}s_{1}\in\{1,10,20,50,100\} and s2∈{1,5,10,20}s_{2}\in\{1,5,10,20\}, and RAIN hyperparameters are tuned over η∈{0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,1}\eta\in\{0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,1\}, λ∈{0.001,0.01,0.1,1}\lambda\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1,1\}, and γ∈{0.001,0.01,0.1,1}\gamma\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1,1\}. SGDA and SEG step-sizes were tuned over α∈{0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,1}\alpha\in\{0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1,1\}, the same step-size grid as RAIN. We run each experiment with 10 independent random seeds and report the average residual norm ‖F⁡(xk)‖\left\|{\mathbb{F}}(x_{k})\right\| together with the shaded region indicating the empirical 5th–95th percentile band.

Experiment 1: Worst-case nonexpansive operator.

We use the affine lower-bound construction of [40]: define H:Rd→Rd{\mathbb{H}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} by H⁡(x1,…,xd)=(xd−2d,−x1,−x2,…,−xd−1){\mathbb{H}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})=\left(x_{d}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{d}},-x_{1},-x_{2},\dots,-x_{d-1}\right), and after choosing a shift vector s∈Rds\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, let F⁡(x)=H⁡(x−s)+(x−s){\mathbb{F}}(x)={\mathbb{H}}(x-s)+(x-s) and T=I−F{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{I}}-{\mathbb{F}}. Then F{\mathbb{F}} is 12\frac{1}{2}-cocoercive and T{\mathbb{T}} is nonexpansive. We use Gaussian noise oracle F^​(x,ξ)=F​(x)+ξ\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(x;\xi)={\mathbb{F}}(x)+\xi with ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2d​Id)\xi\sim{\mathcal{N}}\left(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{d}I_{d}\right), and use a budget of 20002000 samples. We set d=2001d=2001, x0=0x_{0}=0, α=1\alpha=1, σ=0.1\sigma=0.1 and s∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)s\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{d}).

The left panel of Figure 1 illustrates that S-Dual-OHM is not an anytime algorithm, so its intermediate residuals can be worse than those of the other algorithms; however, in the end, it achieves the smallest last-iterate residual among all algorithms compared. This is in sharp contrast with S-OHM with constant BB, which fails to converge and exhibits diverging residual. This demonstrates that Halpern-type algorithms can indeed be prone to accumulation of stochastic errors. However, with variance reduction (Halpern-PAGE) or recursively adjusted anchor (RAIN), the residual convergence gets stabilized. Finally, SEG and SGDA converge steadily although they were not specifically designed for residual minimization.

Experiment 2: Finite-sum cocoercive operator.

We consider a finite-sum problem

F(x)=1n∑i=1nFi(x),Fi(x)=(qi(qi⊤x1:r)0)∈Rd,{\mathbb{F}}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{F}}_{i}(x),\qquad{\mathbb{F}}_{i}(x)=\begin{pmatrix}q_{i}(q_{i}^{\top}x_{1:r})\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{d},

where each qi∈Rrq_{i}\in\mathbb R^{r} is sampled uniformly from the unit sphere. Here each Fi{\mathbb{F}}_{i} is 11-cocoercive and linear, and therefore F{\mathbb{F}} is cocoercive with L≤1L\leq 1 but not strongly monotone when r<dr<d since the common null space of Fi{\mathbb{F}}_{i} is nontrivial. A stochastic oracle call samples component indices and returns the average of the queried Fi{\mathbb{F}}_{i}’s. The operator variance is bounded over the region that trajectories of all algorithms stay within during all experiment runs. We use a budget of 2000 stochastic samples, and set n=200n=200, d=200d=200, r=199r=199 and T=I−α​F{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}} with α=1\alpha=1. We take x0∼10⋅𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{0}\sim 10\cdot{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{d}). This is a generic, non-worst-case problem that basic methods like SGDA can solve effectively. Still, S-Dual-OHM is also fairly competent, and importantly, outperforms its primal counterpart S-OHM. Notably, Halpern-VR-Finite makes very small progress because the total sample budget 2000 is restrictive with our choice n=200n=200, even though it has the best asymptotic dependence on ϵ\epsilon in theory.

Experiment 3: SCSC minimax problem with Huber-type regularizers.

We consider

Φ⁡(x,y)=(1−δ)​∑igν​(xi)+δ​x⊤​y−(1−δ)​∑igν​(yi)+μ2​‖x‖2−μ2​‖y‖2,\Phi(x,y)=(1-\delta)\sum_{i}g_{\nu}(x_{i})+\delta x^{\top}y-(1-\delta)\sum_{i}g_{\nu}(y_{i})+\frac{\mu}{2}\left\|x\right\|^{2}-\frac{\mu}{2}\left\|y\right\|^{2},

for z=(x,y)∈Rd×Rdz=(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, where gν​(u)={12​u2,|u|≤νν​|u|−12​ν2,|u|>νg_{\nu}(u)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}u^{2},&|u|\leq\nu\\ \nu|u|-\frac{1}{2}\nu^{2},&|u|>\nu\end{cases}. The saddle operator F⁡(z)=(∇xΦ​(x,y),−∇yΦ​(x,y)){\mathbb{F}}(z)=(\nabla_{x}\Phi(x,y),-\nabla_{y}\Phi(x,y)) is then given as F⁡(z)=((1−δ)​clip⁡(x,−ν,ν)+δ​y+μ​x−δ​x+(1−δ)​clip⁡(y,−ν,ν)+μ​y){\mathbb{F}}(z)=\begin{pmatrix}(1-\delta)\operatorname{clip}(x,-\nu,\nu)+\delta y+\mu x\\ -\delta x+(1-\delta)\operatorname{clip}(y,-\nu,\nu)+\mu y\end{pmatrix}, which is μ\mu-strongly monotone and MM-Lipschitz with M=1+μM=1+\mu. We use the Gaussian noise oracle F^​(z,ξ)=F​(z)+ξ\widehat{\mathbb{F}}(z;\xi)={\mathbb{F}}(z)+\xi with ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ22​d​I2​d)\xi\sim{\mathcal{N}}\left(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2d}I_{2d}\right), and use a budget of 10000 stochastic samples. We set d=50d=50, δ=10−2\delta=10^{-2}, ν=5×10−5\nu=5\times 10^{-5}, μ=0.1\mu=0.1, L=M2μL=\frac{M^{2}}{\mu} and z0=(x0,y0)z_{0}=(x_{0},y_{0}) is a uniform random unit vector. We use α=1L\alpha=\frac{1}{L} for S-Dual-OHM, S-OHM and Halpern-PAGE.

We simulate both low noise (σ=0.05\sigma=0.05) and high noise (σ=1.5\sigma=1.5) regimes. When σ=0.05\sigma=0.05, we observe rapid progression in earlier iterations of S-Dual-OHM, but then it stagnates (Figure 2). This is because the noise term is small, so the best batch size choice is B∗=1B^{*}=1, i.e., mini-batching does not benefit the final convergence. In this regime, RAIN, SGDA, SEG converges more steadily than S-Dual-OHM, although we still observe that S-OHM is inferior to S-Dual-OHM. With larger noise with σ=1.5\sigma=1.5, we observe that mini-batching becomes effective and B∗=10B^{*}=10 is selected; in this case, dual-anchor with mini-batching exhibits comparable performance to classical methods and deliberately designed near-optimal algorithm RAIN.

6 Conclusion and Open Questions

We demonstrate that dual-anchor acceleration from deterministic root-finding or fixed-point problems admits a direct stochastic extension, unlike anchor-type accelerated algorithms. This is based on the observation that distinct deterministic accelerations are intrinsically different in their behavior under stochasticity. We believe that our work enables interesting future work on acceleration and optimal complexities for stochastic optimization.

Two immediate limitations of our work, which thus remain as open questions, are: (1) whether the dual-anchor mechanism extends to root-finding problems with monotone and Lipschitz operators F{\mathbb{F}} and (2) whether we can further improve the complexity to the optimal level [12] 𝒪⁡(ϵ−2​log⁡ϵ−1){\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2}\log\epsilon^{-1}) via dual-anchor acceleration. As the dual-anchor acceleration also exists in the monotone Lipschitz inclusion setting [54], we believe that the extension would be possible with novel insights not relying on nonexpansivity of I−α​F{\mathbb{I}}-\alpha{\mathbb{F}}. We also expect our result to serve as a baseline that can be combined with broader techniques in stochastic optimization for potentially achieving the optimal complexity.

Appendix B Additional Experiments

In the experiments of Section 5, we used for S-OHM the same batch size BB selected for S-Dual-OHM. This was designed to isolate the effect of replacing the anchor update by the dual-anchor update while keeping all the other configurations identical. However, to verify that the observed empirical advantage of S-Dual-OHM is not an artifact of this experiment design, we repeat all four experiments while separately tuning the batch size of S-OHM over the same grid B∈{1,10,20,50,100}B\in\{1,10,20,50,100\}, under the same total sample budget Q=N​BQ=NB. All the other experimental settings are unchanged. For simplicity, we only compare the results from S-Dual-OHM with tuned BB and runs of S-OHM using the shared and tuned batch sizes.

As shown in Figure 3, independent tuning selects the same batch size for S-OHM and S-Dual-OHM in Experiment 2 and the low-variance regime in Experiment 3. In Experiment 1 and the high-variance regime in Experiment 3, the batch sizes independently chosen for S-OHM differ. Nevertheless, even with its own optimized batch size, the final residual attained by S-OHM remains strictly larger than that of S-Dual-OHM. These results from controlled experiments further supports the empirical benefit/robustness of the dual-anchor mechanism over anchoring in stochastic settings.
